newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria raises 3 bln ATS in fresh capital. [corrected 7:52 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria raises 3 bln ATS in fresh capital. [corrected 7:52 gmt]

text.p: Bank Austria said on Friday it would issue eight million preference shares at a price of 376 schillings each in a public tender from June 9-23 to raise three billion schillings in fresh equity capital.
The new issue was priced at a 10 percent discount to Thursday's close of 416 schillings.

Shareholders of Bank Austria would be offered seven new shares for every 57 preference or common shares already held, the nation's top bank said in a statement published in Vienna daily Wiener Zeitung. The new shares are elegible for dividend payments from July 1st.
(Corrects to make clear offer applies to holders of both common and preference shares).
Holders of the bank's participation shares would be offered seven participation certificates at a price of 329 schilligs each for every 57 certificates already held, the bank added.
The bank in January acquired majority control of its closest competitor, Creditanstalt, for some 17 billion schillings to create Europe's 30th largest banking group in terms of assets.
The bank did not release any news on an eagerly awaited exchange offer to Creditanstalt shareholders.
Bank Austria's planned privatisation has become the object of an increasingly heated political debate in the country.
On Thursday, Social Democrat Chancellor Viktor Klima won a no-confidence vote called by the opposition far-right Freedom Party over the removal of Bank Austria from state control.

The motion was sparked by allegations that Klima backed Bank Austria's acquisition of rival Creditanstalt in the knowledge that Germany's Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale already had first option on a 45.15 percent Bank Austria voting stake currently held by the City of Vienna holding company AVZ.
Vienna city hall is dominated by Social Democrats.

The reduction of AVZ's stake in Bank Austria as well as the eventual sale of the government's 19 percent stake in the bank was a key ingredient of the Creditanstalt deal, Austria's longest running privatisation project since World War Two.
Klima insisted he knew nothing about the deal, which was originally struck in 1995 when WestLB acquired a 10.7 percent voting stake in Bank Austria.
Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa on Thursday warned the political dispute was damaging to the bank's image and had already undermined investor confidence. -- Vienna newsroom +431 53112 274
